findings: The answer separates immediate stop-the-bleeding, consumer recovery, backlog catch-up, replay, reconciliation and prevention rather than treating restart as sufficient.
It does not assume a particular MQ vendor and makes checkpoint, ordering, retry/DLQ and capacity choices conditional on actual pipeline semantics.
MySQL primary documentation bounds replay/retention claims and prevents assuming required binlog history always remains available.
The executable repair invariant blocks duplicate/stale overwrite and stale resurrection after deletes, including a newer authoritative DB reconciliation.
TTL is correctly framed as a bounded-staleness safety net rather than a correctness protocol.
The candidate explicitly distinguishes correctness restoration from throughput catch-up and calls for lag plus reconciliation evidence before declaring recovery.
